# Garage Door Spring Replacement: Cost, Signs, and What to Expect

Garage door spring replacement costs $150 to $350 professionally. Learn the signs your spring is failing, what type you have, and why this is never a DIY repair.

TL;DR

A broken garage door spring is not a DIY repair. Torsion springs are wound under extreme mechanical tension and have caused broken bones, facial injuries, and fatalities when mishandled. Professional replacement costs $150 to $350 for a standard torsion spring set, takes under an hour, and comes with a warranty. If one spring breaks, replace both at the same time. When you replace, ask about high-cycle springs rated for 25,000 cycles. They cost $50 to $100 more and last twice as long.

There was a loud bang from the garage. Now the door will not open. Your car might be inside. You have no idea what just happened or how serious it is.

Here is what happened: your garage door spring broke. And here is the most important thing to know right now: do not press the opener button again. The opener motor is not designed to lift the door without spring tension. Every time you press that button, you risk burning out the motor and turning a $250 spring replacement into a $600 spring-plus-opener replacement. Stop pressing the button. Read the callout box below. Then work through this guide.

Garage door springs are the single most stressed mechanical component in the average home. A standard torsion spring opens and closes 4 times per day, 365 days per year, for 7 years before reaching its rated cycle count. Every cycle winds and unwinds hundreds of foot-pounds of stored energy. When that spring reaches the end of its life, it does not slow down gradually. It fails suddenly, usually with a sound like a gunshot, and the door becomes a 150 to 400 lb unsupported slab that cannot be safely opened until the spring is replaced.

## Critical First Step: Do Not Operate the Door

### Critical Safety Warning

If you suspect a broken spring, stop using the door immediately. Do not press the opener button. The opener motor is designed to move a counterbalanced door, not lift its full weight. Running the opener on a door with a broken spring strains the motor to the point of burning it out, adding a $200 to $400 opener repair to an already urgent situation. If your car is trapped inside, see the emergency manual opening section below for how to open the door safely.

## Torsion Springs vs Extension Springs: Which Do You Have?

Identifying your spring type before calling a professional ensures you get an accurate quote and understand what the job involves. The two types operate differently, have different lifespans, different costs, and different risk profiles.

### How to Identify Your Spring Type

**Look above the door.** If you see a single large coiled spring mounted horizontally on a metal shaft directly above the door opening, you have a torsion spring. This is the most common type in homes built after the mid-1990s.

**Look along the horizontal tracks.** If you see two springs running parallel to the horizontal track sections on either side of the door, one on each side, you have extension springs. These are found on older homes and lighter doors.

Torsion springs mount above the door on a horizontal shaft (left). Extension springs run along the horizontal tracks on each side (right).

Feature| Torsion Spring| Extension Spring
---|---|---
Location| Above the door on a horizontal shaft| Along the horizontal tracks, one per side
How it works| Twists (torques) to store energy| Stretches to store energy
Lifespan| 10,000 to 20,000 cycles (7 to 15 years)| 5,000 to 10,000 cycles (5 to 7 years)
Replacement cost (professional)| $200 to $350 per job (both springs)| $150 to $250 per job (both springs)
If it breaks| Contained on the shaft, door stops| Can become a projectile if no safety cable
Safety| Safer (contained failure)| Requires safety cables to be safe
Best for| Most residential doors| Lighter doors, older construction

**The upgrade case:** If your garage currently has extension springs, replacement is an opportunity to upgrade to torsion springs. The conversion costs $400 to $800 but gives you a longer-lasting, safer system that is gentler on the opener and tracks. Ask your technician about it during the service call.

## What a Broken Spring Looks Like

### Before It Breaks: Warning Signs

Most springs give warning before they snap. Catching these signs early means you can schedule a non-emergency replacement on your timeline instead of dealing with a sudden failure.

**The door feels heavier than usual.** Disconnect the opener by pulling the red emergency release cord and try lifting the door manually. A properly balanced door with healthy springs should feel nearly weightless and stay open on its own at any height. If it takes significant effort to lift, or if the door slowly descends when you let go, the springs are losing tension and are near end-of-life.

**The opener strains or runs longer than usual.** When springs weaken, the opener motor works harder to compensate. If your opener sounds more labored than it used to, or if the door moves more slowly than normal, weakening springs are the most likely cause.

**Visible gaps between coils.** Look at the torsion spring above the door. Healthy spring coils are tightly wound and touching. If you can see daylight between any coils, even a small separation of 1/4 inch. The spring is stretching under load and is near failure. This is the most reliable visual indicator.

**Rust or corrosion on the coils.** Surface rust accelerates metal fatigue. A rusted spring reaches the end of its life faster than a clean spring of the same cycle rating. Lubricating the spring with silicone spray twice per year slows rust formation significantly.

**The door is more than 7 years old and you have never replaced the springs.** Standard torsion springs are rated for 10,000 cycles. At 4 uses per day, that equals 2,500 days or roughly 7 years. If your springs are approaching or past this age, budget for proactive replacement rather than waiting for the bang.

### After It Breaks: What You Will See

A broken torsion spring is usually unmistakable. The indicators are:

  * A loud bang from the garage, often described as a gunshot or car backfire, that occurred while the door was closing or sitting closed
  * The door will not open, or opens only 2 to 4 inches before the opener strains and stops
  * The door feels extremely heavy when you try to lift it manually after disconnecting the opener
  * A visible gap of 2 to 3 inches in the torsion spring coil above the door
  * The lift cables on one or both sides appear slack or have fallen off their drums. A broken spring frequently causes the lift cable to go slack or snap under the uneven load. If your cable also failed, see our [garage door cable broke guide](/problems/garage-door-cable-broke) for what to do next.
  * The door appears crooked or lopsided (more common with extension spring failure on one side). A broken spring can also cause the door to come off its tracks. See our [garage door off track guide](/problems/garage-door-off-track) for diagnosis and repair steps.

## The Cycle Count: What 10,000 Cycles Actually Means for Your Household

Every spring is rated by the number of cycles it can complete before failure. One cycle is one complete open-and-close operation. Standard springs are rated at 10,000 cycles. High-cycle springs are rated at 25,000 to 50,000 cycles.

The translation to years depends entirely on how often you use the door:

Daily Uses| Cycles Per Year| Standard Spring Life| High-Cycle Spring Life
---|---|---|---
2 (one car, basic use)| 730| 13.7 years| 34 to 68 years
4 (typical household)| 1,460| 6.8 years| 17 to 34 years
6 (busy household, two cars)| 2,190| 4.6 years| 11 to 23 years
8 (home office, frequent use)| 2,920| 3.4 years| 8 to 17 years
10+ (garage as primary entrance)| 3,650+| Under 3 years| 7 to 14 years

**The high-cycle upgrade:** When a technician replaces your springs, ask specifically for high-cycle springs rated for 25,000 cycles. The upcharge is typically $50 to $100 over standard springs. For a household using the door 4 times per day, that $75 upgrade buys you an additional 10 or more years before the next replacement. It is almost always worth the money.

## Why This Is Never a DIY Repair

Most home repairs have a reasonable DIY path. Garage door spring replacement does not. This is not a liability disclaimer. It is specific, documented information about what actually happens when this repair goes wrong.

**The energy stored in a torsion spring is substantial.** A standard residential torsion spring exerts over 200 lbs of force when fully wound. The winding process requires inserting steel bars into the winding cone and turning them multiple times while the spring is under this tension. If the bar slips out of the cone at any point during winding or unwinding, it spins with the full rotational force of the spring behind it.

**The documented injuries from DIY spring replacement include:**

  * Broken fingers and hands (the most common injury; hands stay near the winding cone throughout the process)
  * Facial fractures and broken orbital bones from winding bars striking the face
  * Dental damage and concussions from winding bar strikes
  * Deep lacerations from spring coils catching skin during rotation
  * Crush injuries when the door falls unexpectedly during installation

**The tools required are not commonly owned.** Proper spring replacement requires hardened steel winding bars of a specific diameter and length (18 to 24 inches, 5/8 inch diameter). Using any substitute (a screwdriver, a piece of rebar, a pipe) dramatically increases the risk of slippage. These bars are not sold at standard hardware stores. Purchasing them adds $30 to $60 to the DIY cost.

**The cost math does not favor DIY.** A spring set costs $50 to $100 for parts. Add winding bars ($30 to $60), the time to correctly size the replacement spring to your door's weight (requires measuring wire diameter, inside diameter, and spring length), and the real risk of incorrect installation causing the spring to fail early or the door to go off-balance. Professional installation costs $150 to $350 total, includes correct sizing, and comes with a warranty on parts and labor. The math rarely favors DIY even before accounting for the medical risk.

## What Garage Door Spring Replacement Costs in 2026

Scenario| Cost Range| Notes
---|---|---
Single torsion spring, standard cycle| $150 to $250| Rare; most doors have two springs
Both torsion springs, standard cycle| $200 to $350| The most common scenario
Both torsion springs, high-cycle upgrade| $250 to $450| Recommended; extends life significantly
Extension springs, both sides| $150 to $250| Includes safety cables if not present
Emergency/after-hours call| Add $50 to $100| After-hours premium on top of regular rate
Extension to torsion conversion| $400 to $800| Full system change, labor intensive
Springs plus cables (if cables damaged)| Add $75 to $150| Common when a spring breaks suddenly

**Labor breakdown:** Labor typically runs $75 to $150 per hour. Spring replacement takes 45 to 90 minutes for a standard job. The technician also performs a full balance test, adjusts the opener's force settings to match the new spring tension, and lubricates all moving parts.

**Getting a fair quote:** Call at least two companies. Be specific: tell them you have a broken torsion spring (or extension spring), your door size (single or double, height), and whether your car is trapped. Most reputable companies give a price range over the phone. Be wary of companies that refuse to quote without an in-person inspection for a standard spring replacement.

If your spring repair quotes are pushing past 50 percent of new door replacement cost, replacement is usually the smarter financial decision. Use our [garage door cost calculator](/cost-guides/garage-door-replacement-cost-calculator) to get a quick installed estimate so you can compare against the repair quote and decide.

## How to Open the Door Manually When a Spring Is Broken

If your car is inside and you need to get it out before the technician arrives, here is how to open the door safely with a broken spring. This requires two strong adults.

**Step 1:** Disconnect the opener by pulling the red emergency release cord hanging from the ceiling rail.

**Step 2:** Stand on either side of the door, one person per side. Place hands at the bottom corners of the door.

**Step 3:** Lift together in a controlled, steady motion. With a broken spring, the door will feel its full weight (150 to 400 lbs depending on door type). This is a two-person lift. Do not attempt alone.

**Step 4:** Once open, prop the door with a solid object placed under each bottom corner. The door will not stay open on its own without spring tension. Clamps on the track above the rollers are the safest option.

**Step 5:** Back the vehicle out, then slowly lower the door together. Do not let the door fall.

After this, do not operate the door again until the springs are replaced.

## What Happens During a Professional Spring Replacement

Understanding the process helps you evaluate what a technician tells you and ensures you are getting the full service, not just the spring swap.

**Step 1: Diagnosis and sizing.** The technician measures the existing spring (wire diameter, inside diameter, length, and wind direction) to identify the correct replacement. They also inspect the cables, drums, bearings, and rollers for wear while the door is down.

**Step 2: Tension release.** The existing spring tension is released using hardened steel winding bars. Even a broken spring retains partial tension that must be released safely before removal.

**Step 3: Spring removal.** The broken spring is slid off the torsion bar (or unhooked from the extension spring track mount) and removed.

**Step 4: New spring installation.** The replacement spring is installed and wound to the correct tension for the door's weight. The number of turns is calculated based on the door height and spring specifications.

**Step 5: Balance test.** The door is disconnected from the opener and lifted manually to 3 to 4 feet. It should hold its position. If it rises or falls, the spring tension is adjusted.

**Step 6: Opener reconnection and adjustment.** The opener is reconnected and the force settings are adjusted to match the new spring tension. A properly balanced door requires almost no opener effort.

**Step 7: Safety test.** The auto-reverse test is performed (2x4 on the ground test) to confirm the opener safety mechanism is functioning correctly.

A quality technician completes all seven steps. If a company only does steps 3 and 4 and calls it done, you have not received a complete service.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does it cost to replace a garage door spring?

Professional replacement of both torsion springs costs $200 to $350 for a standard set, or $250 to $450 if you upgrade to high-cycle springs rated for 25,000 cycles. Extension spring replacement runs $150 to $250 for both sides. After-hours or emergency service adds $50 to $100. Parts alone cost $50 to $100, but the labor, correct sizing, balance testing, and warranty that come with professional service make DIY a poor trade-off for most homeowners.

### How do I know if my garage door spring is broken?

The clearest signs are a loud bang from the garage (the spring snapping under tension), the door refusing to open or opening only 2 to 4 inches, the door feeling extremely heavy when you try to lift it manually after disconnecting the opener, and a visible 2 to 3 inch gap in the torsion spring coil above the door. Slack or fallen lift cables on either side of the door are also a strong indicator that a spring has failed.

### Can I replace a garage door spring myself?

No. Torsion spring replacement is one of the most dangerous DIY repairs a homeowner can attempt. The springs store over 200 lbs of mechanical force. If a winding bar slips during installation, it spins with the full rotational force of the spring, causing broken bones, facial fractures, and in documented cases, fatalities. The [Consumer Product Safety Commission](https://www.cpsc.gov/FAQ/Automatic-Residential-Garage-Door-Operators) tracks over 20,000 garage door related emergency room visits annually. Professional replacement costs $150 to $350 and takes under an hour. The cost savings of DIY do not justify the injury risk.

### Do I need to replace both springs if only one breaks?

Yes. Both springs were installed at the same time and have completed the same number of cycles. When one breaks, the other is statistically near the end of its life. Replacing only the broken spring leaves you with one new spring and one aging spring, creating an unbalanced door and a second failure within months. Technicians price both springs together because the labor cost is nearly identical for one or two, making dual replacement the clear value choice.

### How long do garage door springs last?

Standard torsion springs are rated for 10,000 cycles and last 7 years at 4 uses per day. High-cycle springs rated for 25,000 cycles last 17 years at the same usage rate. Extension springs are rated for 5,000 to 10,000 cycles and last 5 to 7 years. Lifespan varies significantly with usage frequency. A garage used as the primary entrance with 8 uses per day will wear through a standard spring in under 4 years.

### What is a high-cycle spring and is it worth it?

A high-cycle spring is a torsion spring rated for 25,000 cycles or more instead of the standard 10,000. It is made from a higher grade of steel with a tighter wire tolerance. The upcharge over a standard spring is typically $50 to $100. For a household using the door 4 times per day, upgrading from a 10,000-cycle spring to a 25,000-cycle spring buys an additional 10 or more years before the next replacement. It is almost always worth the money and should be requested proactively when scheduling replacement.

### What causes garage door springs to break?

Metal fatigue from repeated stress cycles is the primary cause. Every open-and-close winds and unwinds the spring, creating microscopic stress fractures in the steel that accumulate over thousands of cycles. Cold weather accelerates failure because steel contracts in low temperatures, increasing internal stress. Rust and corrosion thin the spring wire and concentrate stress at corroded points. Lack of lubrication increases friction and heat during operation. Springs that were undersized for the door's weight from the original installation fail faster because they are under greater stress per cycle.

### Is it safe to use the garage door with a weakened spring?

No. A spring that is losing tension but has not yet broken creates an unbalanced door that puts excessive strain on the opener motor, cables, and rollers. The opener was designed to move a counterbalanced door with minimal effort. When it has to compensate for spring loss, it wears out significantly faster. A weakened spring also increases the risk of a sudden failure while the door is in motion, which is more dangerous than a failure in the closed position. If the manual lift test reveals a heavier-than-normal door, schedule replacement before the spring fails.

## Glossary

Torsion spring

A large coiled spring mounted horizontally on a metal shaft above the garage door opening. It stores mechanical energy by twisting (torquing) as the door closes and releases that energy to assist opening. Standard torsion springs are rated for 10,000 cycles. High-cycle versions run 25,000 to 50,000 cycles. Torsion springs are safer than extension springs because when they break, they remain contained on the shaft rather than becoming projectiles.

Extension spring

Two springs mounted along the horizontal track sections on either side of the garage door, running parallel to the ceiling. They store energy by stretching as the door closes. Extension springs are rated for 5,000 to 10,000 cycles and are generally found on older homes and lighter doors. Safety cables threaded through each spring prevent them from becoming projectiles if they snap.

Cycle

One complete open-and-close operation of the garage door. Spring lifespan is measured in cycles rather than years because usage frequency determines wear rate. At 4 uses per day (2 opens and 2 closes), a garage door completes 1,460 cycles per year. A 10,000-cycle spring lasts approximately 6.8 years at this rate.

High-cycle spring

A torsion spring manufactured from higher-grade steel and rated for 25,000 to 50,000 cycles instead of the standard 10,000. The upcharge over standard springs is $50 to $100 per replacement job. For most households, the extended lifespan makes high-cycle springs the better long-term value. They should be requested proactively when scheduling replacement.

Winding bar

A hardened steel rod, 18 to 24 inches long and 5/8 inch in diameter, inserted into the winding cone of a torsion spring to wind or unwind it during installation. Using any substitute (screwdrivers, rebar, pipe) dramatically increases the risk of the bar slipping and causing injury. Winding bars are the primary tool that separates professional spring replacement from amateur attempts.

Winding cone

The metal cone-shaped fitting at each end of a torsion spring where the winding bars are inserted during installation. The cone has holes or slots for the bars and set screws that lock the spring tension in place. Incorrect use of the winding cone is the primary point of failure in DIY spring replacement attempts.

Safety cable

A steel cable threaded through the center of each extension spring, anchored at both ends. If the extension spring breaks or comes unhooked, the safety cable contains it and prevents it from flying across the garage. Homes with extension springs that lack safety cables should have them added during any spring service visit.

Balance test

A diagnostic check performed after spring installation to verify correct tension. The door is disconnected from the opener and lifted manually to 3 to 4 feet, then released. A properly balanced door holds its position. A door that rises means the spring is over-tensioned; one that falls means under-tensioned. Both conditions require adjustment before the opener is reconnected.

Counterbalance

The principle by which garage door springs offset the weight of the door, making it feel nearly weightless when opening and closing. A properly counterbalanced door requires minimal force from the opener motor. When springs fail, the counterbalance is lost and the full weight of the door (150 to 400 lbs) must be managed manually or by the opener, which is not designed for that load.

# Garage Door Weather Stripping: When to Replace It and How to Do It Right

Garage door weather stripping replacement guide. Signs it has failed, which of the 4 seals to replace, costs, and step-by-step DIY installation for each type.

GG

The Garage Guide

Updated Mar 2026 · 12 min read

Problem

TL;DR

A garage door has four separate weather seals: the bottom seal, two side seals, and the top seal. Each fails at a different rate and requires a different replacement approach. The bottom seal fails most often and costs $20 to $45 to replace yourself in 20 minutes. A full perimeter replacement (all four seals) costs $50 to $120 in materials and takes 60 to 90 minutes. The clearest sign any seal has failed: you can see daylight around the closed door, feel airflow with your hand, or find water, dust, or pests inside after the door has been closed.

Something is getting into your garage that should not be. Water after a rainstorm. A draft in winter that makes the space 15 degrees colder than it should be. A mouse that found a gap you cannot see. Or just dust accumulating faster than makes sense for a closed space.

In almost every case, the answer is the weather stripping. These four rubber and vinyl seals are the only thing standing between your garage interior and the outside world, and they are also the most overlooked maintenance item on any garage door. Most homeowners replace springs, openers, and even panels while worn weather stripping quietly lets in cold air, moisture, and pests for years.

This guide covers all four seals, how to identify which one has failed, what to replace it with, and exactly how to install each type.

## The Daylight Test: Start Here

### Critical First Test

Close the garage door completely and go inside. Turn off the garage lights and wait 30 seconds for your eyes to adjust. Look around the full perimeter of the door (bottom, both sides, and top). Any light visible means air, water, and pests can also get in at that point. Then press the back of your hand against the bottom seal while someone stands outside. Any airflow you feel confirms the bottom seal has failed. This test takes two minutes and tells you exactly which seals need replacing before you spend a dollar on materials.

## The Four Seals: What Each One Does and Where It Lives

Most articles treat garage door weather stripping as a single item. It is actually four distinct components, each in a different location, each with a different failure mode, and each requiring a different replacement product.

Seal| Location| What It Prevents| Typical Lifespan| DIY Replacement Cost
---|---|---|---|---
Bottom seal (astragal)| Underside of door| Water, air, pests, debris from floor gap| 3 to 5 years| $20 to $45
Side seals (stop molding)| Door frame, left and right| Air and water infiltration along door edges| 5 to 7 years| $15 to $30 per side
Top seal (header seal)| Door frame above door| Air and water from above| 5 to 7 years| $15 to $25
Panel seals (between sections)| Between horizontal door panels| Air infiltration through panel joints| 10 to 15 years| Replaced with door

**The bottom seal fails most often** because it is the only seal that contacts the ground on every single cycle. It gets compressed, scraped, frozen to the floor in winter, torn by ice, and degraded by UV. At 4 cycles per day, that is 1,460 contact events per year.

**The side and top seals** fail more slowly because they are not subject to ground contact, but UV exposure and temperature cycling make them brittle over 5 to 7 years.

**Panel seals** (the interlocking rubber sections between door panels) last the longest and are generally not replaced independently. They are part of the door panel itself.

## Signs Each Seal Has Failed

### Bottom Seal Failure Signs

  * Visible daylight under the door when closed
  * Water pooling inside after rain or snow melt
  * Insects, rodents, or debris inside a closed garage
  * The seal looks flattened, cracked, torn, or missing sections
  * A chunk of rubber found on the garage floor (a piece tore off during opening)
  * The door froze to the floor overnight and the seal tore when the opener pulled it up

### Side and Top Seal Failure Signs

  * Daylight visible along the sides or top of the closed door
  * Drafts felt along the door frame edges (run your hand slowly along the frame with the door closed)
  * The rubber or vinyl is visibly cracked, brittle, or pulling away from the frame
  * Water staining on the interior door frame after heavy rain
  * The seal no longer springs back when you compress it (has permanently flattened)

### The 5-Year Rule

Regardless of visible symptoms, replace all weather stripping when the bottom seal reaches 5 years old. All four seals were likely installed at the same time and have experienced the same UV and temperature exposure. Replacing the bottom seal alone when the perimeter seals are also aging just delays the next replacement by one or two years. Doing all four at once takes 90 minutes total and costs $50 to $120 in materials. For a full seasonal inspection schedule that includes weather seal checks, see the [garage door maintenance checklist](/guides/garage-door-maintenance).

## Choosing the Right Bottom Seal

The bottom seal is the most critical and the most confusing to replace because there are multiple profile types and they are not interchangeable. Buying the wrong profile means the seal will not fit the retainer on the bottom of your door.

**How to identify your profile:** Look at the aluminum retainer on the bottom of the door. The retainer has a channel or slot that the seal slides into. Match the seal to the channel shape:

Profile Type| Retainer Shape| Best For
---|---|---
T-slot (T-end)| T-shaped channel| Most common residential door, flat floors
Bulb seal| Open-face retainer or adhesive mount| Smooth concrete floors, standard gaps
J-type| J-shaped channel| Older doors, specific manufacturer fitments
Beaded (P-type)| Round-channel retainer| Some Wayne Dalton, Clopay models

**If you cannot identify the profile:** Slide the old seal out of the retainer (it slides from one end) and take it to the hardware store for matching. Alternatively, take a photo of the bottom of the door with the retainer visible and use it to search the manufacturer's replacement parts.

**Material choice:**

  * **EPDM rubber:** Best overall. Remains flexible in cold temperatures down to -40 degrees Fahrenheit, UV resistant, longest lifespan. Costs $5 to $10 more than vinyl but lasts significantly longer.
  * **Vinyl (PVC):** Less expensive. Adequate in mild climates. Becomes brittle in sustained cold below 20 degrees Fahrenheit. Good choice if budget is the primary consideration and you are in a warm climate.
  * **Silicone:** Premium option. Excellent UV resistance and temperature range. Costs $10 to $15 more than EPDM. Worthwhile for south-facing doors with heavy direct sun exposure.

## How to Replace the Bottom Seal

**Tools needed:** Flathead screwdriver, utility knife, measuring tape, silicone spray

**Time:** 20 to 30 minutes

**Cost:** $20 to $45 for the seal

  1. **Disconnect the opener** by pulling the red emergency release cord so the door can be moved manually.
  2. **Open the door to a comfortable working height** (about waist level) and lock it in place by clamping locking pliers on the track above a roller.
  3. **Slide the old seal out** of the aluminum retainer from one end. It slides horizontally. If it is stuck, spray a small amount of silicone lubricant at the entry point and work it free. Do not pry or force. You may need the retainer intact for the new seal.
  4. **Measure the door width precisely.** Most residential doors are 8, 9, 10, 16, or 18 feet. Buy a seal that is at least 2 inches longer than the door width so you can trim to exact fit.
  5. **Slide the new seal into the retainer** from one end, pushing it along until it extends past both sides of the door.
  6. **With the door closed against the floor, trim the seal** with a utility knife so it extends approximately 1/2 inch past each side of the door. This slight overhang ensures full contact at the corners.
  7. **Apply a thin coat of silicone spray** to the bottom of the seal. This prevents the seal from bonding to wet concrete or ice overnight and tearing when the opener pulls the door up in the morning.
  8. **Reconnect the opener and test.** The door should close fully with the seal compressing evenly against the floor.

## How to Replace Side and Top Seals (Stop Molding)

The perimeter seals run along the door frame, up both sides and across the top. They are typically a vinyl or rubber strip stapled or nailed to a wood stop molding, or in newer construction, a self-adhesive foam or rubber strip pressed against the frame.

**Tools needed:** Pry bar or flathead screwdriver, hammer, staple gun or nails, utility knife, measuring tape

**Time:** 30 to 45 minutes for all three runs

**Cost:** $15 to $30 per run, or $40 to $80 for a complete perimeter kit

  1. **With the door closed, examine the existing perimeter seal.** If it is stapled or nailed wood stop molding with a rubber flange, it must be removed and replaced as a unit. If it is a self-adhesive foam or rubber strip, it can be peeled off and replaced without removing the molding.
  2. **Wood stop molding type:** Pry the molding away from the frame carefully, starting at the bottom. Remove all staples or nails. Take a section to the hardware store to match the profile.
  3. **Measure each run** (left side, right side, and top). Add 2 inches to each measurement. Cut the new molding to length with a utility knife or saw.
  4. **With the door closed, press the new molding against the frame** so the rubber flange contacts the door face firmly. Secure with nails or staples every 6 inches. The rubber flange should compress slightly against the door surface. Enough to create a seal but not so much that it resists door movement.
  5. **Test by closing the door** and running your hand along the perimeter. No airflow should be detectable.
  6. **Self-adhesive type:** Clean the frame surface with rubbing alcohol and allow to dry completely. Peel and press the new adhesive seal into position. Press firmly along its full length. Allow 24 hours before testing in wet or cold conditions.

## What Weather Stripping Replacement Actually Costs

Scope| DIY Materials| Professional Installation
---|---|---
Bottom seal only| $20 to $45| $75 to $150
Side seals (both sides)| $30 to $60| $100 to $200
Top seal only| $15 to $25| $75 to $125
Full perimeter (all four positions)| $50 to $120| $150 to $350

**When professional installation is worth it:**

  * The aluminum retainer on the bottom of the door is damaged or bent. Replacing a damaged retainer requires drilling out rivets or removing screws, which is genuinely difficult without experience.
  * The wood stop molding around the frame is rotted. Rotted molding needs to be replaced, not just re-sealed, and is attached to the structural frame.
  * The door itself is warped or out of square. No amount of new weather stripping seals a door that does not sit flat in its frame. If the door is warping due to failing springs, see our [garage door spring replacement guide](/problems/garage-door-spring-replacement).

## Seasonal Maintenance That Extends Seal Life

**Spring:** Inspect all four seals after winter. Winter is the hardest season on weather stripping. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles, ice bonding, and cold-induced brittleness cause more damage than the rest of the year combined. Replace anything that cracked or tore over winter before summer UV exposure makes it worse.

**Summer:** Apply a UV protectant spray (303 Aerospace Protectant or similar) to rubber seals on south or west-facing doors. Direct sun degrades rubber faster than any other factor. A UV spray applied in May extends seal life by one to two years on high-sun exposures.

**Fall:** Apply silicone spray to the bottom seal before the first freeze. This is the single most effective way to prevent the seal from bonding to ice on the concrete floor overnight and tearing when the opener pulls the door up on a cold morning. Takes 30 seconds. See our [garage door winterization guide](/guides/how-to-winterize-your-garage) for the full pre-winter seal checklist.

**Year-round:** Never use petroleum-based lubricants (WD-40, motor oil) on rubber seals. Petroleum degrades rubber over time, accelerating cracking and brittleness. Use only silicone-based products on any rubber component. According to the [U.S. Department of Energy](https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/air-sealing-your-home), proper air sealing is one of the most cost-effective ways to reduce energy loss in any home.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I know if my garage door weather stripping needs replacing?

The clearest signs are visible daylight around the closed door, drafts you can feel with your hand along the door frame, water pooling inside after rain, pests or insects getting in despite a closed door, and visible cracking, brittleness, or missing sections in the rubber or vinyl material. The bottom seal should also be replaced if it froze to the floor and tore during a winter opening. A damaged seal does not recover after tearing.

### How long does garage door weather stripping last?

Bottom seals last 3 to 5 years at average use (4 cycles per day). Side and top seals last 5 to 7 years. Quality EPDM rubber lasts significantly longer than vinyl in cold climates. Properly installed weather stripping with regular silicone spray maintenance and UV protection can reach the higher end of these ranges. Poorly installed seals, or seals on south-facing doors without UV protection, can fail in 2 to 3 years.

### Can I replace garage door weather stripping myself?

Yes, for most homeowners. Bottom seal replacement requires sliding the old seal out and the new one in. No tools beyond a utility knife and tape measure are needed. Side and top seal replacement requires a staple gun or hammer and nails for wood stop molding types. The only situations that genuinely require a professional are a damaged or bent bottom retainer, rotted frame molding, or a door that is warped out of square.

### What is the best material for garage door weather stripping?

EPDM rubber is the best overall choice. It remains flexible in temperatures down to -40 degrees Fahrenheit, resists UV degradation effectively, and outlasts vinyl by several years in cold climates. Vinyl (PVC) is a reasonable budget option in mild climates but becomes brittle in sustained cold below 20 degrees. Silicone is the premium option for high-sun exposures. It handles UV better than EPDM and costs $10 to $15 more per replacement.

### Why does my garage door keep freezing to the floor?

The bottom seal is bonding to water on the concrete floor before it freezes overnight. The fix is simple: apply silicone spray to the bottom of the seal every fall. Silicone prevents rubber from bonding to ice. If the door has already frozen, do not press the opener button. That burns out the motor. Disconnect the opener, chip the ice away from outside, and lift the door manually. See our [garage door won't open guide](/problems/garage-door-wont-open) for the full frozen door procedure.

### How much does it cost to replace garage door weather stripping?

DIY replacement of the bottom seal costs $20 to $45 in materials. A full perimeter replacement (all four seal positions) costs $50 to $120 in materials and takes 60 to 90 minutes. Professional installation of the full perimeter runs $150 to $350 depending on door size and seal condition. The bottom seal is by far the most cost-effective DIY maintenance task on any garage door.

### Should I replace all the weather stripping at once or just the failed piece?

Replace all four seals at the same time when the bottom seal reaches 5 years old. All seals were installed simultaneously and have experienced the same degradation from UV and temperature. Replacing only the failed piece leaves aging seals in place that will require replacement within one to two years anyway. The incremental labor cost of doing all four at once is minimal and the material cost difference is $30 to $50.

### Does garage door weather stripping affect energy bills?

Yes, meaningfully for attached garages. An uninsulated or poorly sealed attached garage acts as a thermal buffer for adjacent rooms. Air infiltration through failed weather stripping is a direct energy loss pathway. According to the Department of Energy, properly sealing and insulating the boundary between an attached garage and living space can reduce energy loss through that wall by 60 to 70 percent. For a detached garage, the energy impact is limited to the garage itself. It is significant if you heat the space and minimal if you do not. For more on insulation and sealing working together, see our [garage insulation guide](/guides/how-to-insulate-garage).

## Glossary

Bottom seal (door astragal)

The rubber or vinyl strip running the full width of the garage door bottom, housed in an aluminum retainer. It creates a weather-tight barrier between the door and the concrete floor on every close cycle. The most frequently replaced weather sealing component on any garage door. Standard lifespan is 3 to 5 years. Profile types (T-slot, bulb, J-type, beaded) are not interchangeable. Match the profile to the retainer before purchasing.

Stop molding

The wood frame trim running up both sides and across the top of the garage door opening, with an attached rubber or vinyl flange that contacts the door face when closed. Provides the side and top seals. Secured to the structural door frame with nails or staples. Replaced as a unit when the rubber flange degrades. Full perimeter replacement kits cost $40 to $80.

EPDM rubber

Ethylene propylene diene monomer rubber, the best material choice for garage door weather seals. Remains flexible at temperatures down to -40 degrees Fahrenheit, resists UV degradation effectively, and outlasts vinyl by several years in cold climates. The correct material for bottom seals in any climate with significant winter temperatures.

T-slot profile

The most common bottom seal profile for residential garage doors. The seal has a T-shaped stem that slides into a matching T-channel in the aluminum retainer on the bottom of the door. Not interchangeable with bulb, J-type, or beaded profiles. Identify your profile by examining the retainer channel before purchasing a replacement.

Retainer

The aluminum extrusion mounted to the bottom of the garage door that holds the bottom seal. The retainer has a specific channel profile (T, J, bulb, or bead) that accepts only the matching seal profile. If the retainer is bent or damaged, the seal cannot seat properly and the retainer must be replaced before the seal. Retainer replacement requires removing mounting hardware and is a more involved repair than seal replacement alone.

Silicone spray lubricant

A dry, non-greasy lubricant appropriate for all rubber seal surfaces. Applied to the bottom seal every fall, it prevents the seal from bonding to ice on the concrete floor overnight. Never use petroleum-based products (WD-40, motor oil) on rubber seals. Petroleum degrades rubber and accelerates cracking and brittleness.

UV protectant

A spray product (such as 303 Aerospace Protectant) that protects rubber and vinyl from UV degradation. Applied to perimeter seals in spring, particularly on south and west-facing doors with heavy direct sun exposure. Extends seal life by one to two years on high-sun exposures. Available at auto parts stores and hardware stores for $10 to $20.

Panel seal

The interlocking rubber gasket integrated between horizontal door panels that prevents air infiltration through panel joints. Unlike perimeter seals, panel seals are part of the door panel itself and are not independently replaceable. They last the longest of any seal type (10 to 15 years) and are replaced when the panel is replaced.

# Garage Door Won't Close? 10 Causes and How to Fix Each One

Six types of symptoms. Ten causes ranked easiest to hardest. Fix costs from $0 to $350.

GG

The Garage Guide

Updated Mar 2026 · 20 min read

Your garage door goes up fine, but refuses to come back down. Or it starts closing and immediately reverses. Or it closes partway and stops. Every guide on the internet tells you to check the sensors. That is cause number one, and it is the most common. But if you have already checked the sensors and the door still will not close, you need the other nine causes that most guides skip.

This guide covers every reason a garage door will not close, ranked from easiest to hardest to fix, with the specific symptoms that identify each cause and what the repair costs. If your opener is not responding at all — no lights, no sounds, nothing — see our [garage door opener not working guide](/problems/garage-door-opener-not-working) instead. This article is specifically for doors where the opener activates, but the door will not complete the closing cycle.

## Quick Diagnostic: What Is Your Door Doing?

Find your symptom. This narrows the cause immediately.

What the Door Does| Most Likely Cause| Jump To
---|---|---
Starts to close, immediately reverses, opener light blinks| Safety sensor blocked, dirty, or misaligned| Cause 1
Starts to close, reverses after a few inches| Safety sensor issue or close-limit setting| Cause 1 or 5
Motor runs but door does not move| Disconnected trolley or broken drive gear| Cause 7 or 8
Door closes partway, then stops and reverses| Track obstruction, damaged roller, or force setting too low| Cause 3, 4, or 6
Remote does not work but wall button does| Dead remote battery or range issue| Cause 2
Neither remote nor wall button closes the door| Sensor wiring issue, power problem, or lock mode engaged| Cause 1, 9, or 10
Door closes unevenly or at an angle| Broken spring, cable, or track issue| Cause 4 or 8
Door makes grinding noise but won't close| Stripped gear, track obstruction, or frozen rollers| Cause 3, 7, or 8

## The 10 Causes, Ranked Easiest to Hardest

### Cause 1: Safety Sensor Problem

Fix: $0 — $50 • Time: 5 to 15 minutes

This is the cause 80% of the time. Every garage door opener manufactured after 1993 has two photo-eye sensors mounted near the floor on either side of the door opening. They send an invisible infrared beam across the opening. If anything breaks that beam, or if the sensors cannot see each other, the door will not close.

Symptoms

  * Door starts to close and immediately reverses
  * Opener light blinks (typically 10 times on LiftMaster/Chamberlain, varies by brand)
  * Wall button works if you press and hold it (bypasses sensors on most models)
  * One or both sensor indicator lights are off or blinking

Fix it in this order:

  1. **Check for obstructions.** Look for anything between the sensors — a broom, a box, a trash can, a spiderweb, a toy. Even a small object or cobweb can break the beam. Remove it and try again.
  2. **Clean the sensor lenses.** Dust, dirt, cobwebs, and moisture film on the sensor lenses block the infrared beam. Wipe both lenses with a soft dry cloth. This alone solves the problem surprisingly often.
  3. **Check alignment.** Both sensors must point directly at each other. The sending sensor (usually amber/yellow LED) and the receiving sensor (usually green LED) should both show steady lights when aligned. If the receiving sensor LED is blinking or off, loosen the wing nut on the mounting bracket, adjust until the green light is steady, and retighten.
  4. **Check the wiring.** Follow the thin wires from each sensor back to the opener unit. Look for damaged, cut, or pinched wires. A wire caught under a roller bracket or chewed by a rodent is a common find. Repair any damage with wire nuts and electrical tape, or replace the wire run.
  5. **Check for sunlight interference.** Direct sunlight hitting the receiving sensor can overwhelm the infrared beam. This typically happens only at specific times of day when the sun angle is low. A cardboard tube taped around the sensor as a shade solves this. Commercial sensor shades are available for $5 to $10.
  6. **Replace the sensors.** If cleaning, aligning, and checking wires does not fix it, the sensor itself may have failed. Replacement sensors cost $15 to $50 depending on brand and are a straightforward swap — two screws and two wire connections per sensor.

According to the [Consumer Product Safety Commission](https://www.cpsc.gov/FAQ/Automatic-Residential-Garage-Door-Operators), safety sensors have been required on all residential garage door openers since 1993. Never bypass them permanently.

### Cause 2: Dead Remote Battery

Fix: $5 • Time: 2 minutes

If the wall button closes the door but the remote does not, the remote battery is dead. This is the simplest possible cause and is easy to overlook.

How to fix it:

Open the back of the remote, replace the battery (usually a CR2032 coin cell), and test. If the remote still does not work after a fresh battery, reprogram it: press the Learn button on the opener unit, then press the remote button within 30 seconds. Check your opener's manual for the specific pairing procedure.

### Cause 3: Track Obstruction or Damage

Fix: $0 — $200 • Time: 15 to 60 minutes

The metal tracks on either side of the door guide the rollers as the door opens and closes. Any obstruction in the track, or any bend or dent in the track itself, can prevent the door from closing.

Symptoms:

  * Door closes partway and stops or binds at a specific point
  * You can see a dent, bend, or foreign object in the track
  * Rollers appear to jam at the same spot every time
  * Door moves unevenly — one side leads the other

How to fix it:

  * **For obstructions:** Inspect both tracks from top to bottom. Remove any debris, screws, small tools, or buildup. A flashlight and a rag handle most cases.
  * **For minor dents or bends:** A rubber mallet can gently tap a small dent back into shape. Do not use a metal hammer. Loosen track brackets if needed to realign, then retighten.
  * **For major damage:** If the track is severely bent, crimped, or separating from the wall, call a professional. Tracks significantly out of alignment can cause the door to fall off, which is a serious safety hazard. Professional track repair or replacement costs $125 to $200 per track.

### Cause 4: Broken Spring or Cable

Fix: $150 — $350 • Professional Only — Do NOT DIY

Garage door springs counterbalance the weight of the door (typically 100 to 200 pounds for a single door, 200 to 400 for a double). When a spring breaks, the opener motor cannot lift or lower that weight alone. The door may close partway and stop, close unevenly, or the motor may strain audibly without moving the door.

Symptoms:

  * A loud bang was heard from the garage (the spring breaking)
  * Door feels extremely heavy when lifted manually
  * Visible gap in the torsion spring above the door
  * One extension spring on the side is hanging loose or broken
  * Door closes crookedly — one side faster than the other
  * A cable is hanging loose or visibly snapped

⚠️ Do NOT attempt spring or cable repair yourself.

Torsion springs are under extreme tension and can cause serious injury or death if they release unexpectedly. This is universally the one garage door repair that every expert says to leave to a professional. A professional spring replacement costs $150 to $350 depending on spring type and door size. Most reputable companies offer same-day service.

While waiting for repair, you can manually close the door by pulling the emergency release cord (the red handle) and carefully lowering the door by hand. Have someone help you as the door will be very heavy without a functioning spring.

### Cause 5: Close-Limit Setting Needs Adjustment

Fix: $0 • Time: 10 minutes

Every garage door opener has a close-limit setting that tells the motor how far down to travel before stopping. If this setting is wrong, the opener thinks the door has hit the ground or an obstacle before it actually has, and it reverses.

Symptoms:

  * Door closes most of the way but reverses right before reaching the floor
  * Door closes to the floor but immediately bounces back up
  * No sensor light blinking (sensors are not the problem)
  * Problem started after a new opener installation or after the opener was serviced

How to fix it:

Locate the limit adjustment screws on the opener unit (usually on the back or side, labeled “open” and “close” or marked with up/down arrows). Turn the close-limit screw in small increments (quarter turns) in the direction that extends the travel distance. Test after each adjustment. On newer smart openers (Chamberlain myQ, LiftMaster, Genie), the limits may be set through the app or a digital interface rather than physical screws.

### Cause 6: Force Setting Too Low

Fix: $0 • Time: 5 minutes

The force setting controls how much resistance the motor will push through before reversing. If set too low, the door reverses at the slightest resistance, including the normal friction of weatherstripping touching the floor.

Symptoms:

  * Door reaches the floor and reverses
  * Door reverses when it meets minor resistance (weatherstripping, slight ice buildup, a leaf)
  * Increasing frequency over time as weatherstripping compresses or tracks accumulate grime

How to fix it:

Locate the force adjustment screw (usually next to the limit screws on the opener, labeled “force” or with a gauge icon). Turn it clockwise in small increments to increase the closing force. Test after each adjustment. The door should close firmly against the floor without bouncing back, but should still reverse if you place your hand or a 2x4 in its path. **If it does not reverse with a solid obstruction, you have set the force too high and need to back it down.** This safety feature must remain functional.

### Cause 7: Stripped Opener Gear

Fix: $15 — $75 DIY • $100 — $200 Pro

Inside the opener, a nylon or plastic drive gear transfers motor power to the chain, belt, or screw drive. Over years of use, this gear wears down and eventually strips. When it strips, the motor runs — you hear it — but the drive mechanism does not move.

Symptoms:

  * Motor activates and runs but the door does not move at all
  * You may hear a grinding or whirring sound
  * The chain, belt, or screw drive is not moving even though the motor is on
  * Problem came on gradually (door was getting slower) or suddenly

How to fix it:

Replacement gear kits are available for $15 to $30 for most major opener brands (Chamberlain, LiftMaster, Genie, Craftsman). The repair involves opening the opener housing and swapping the gear. It is a moderate DIY project that takes 1 to 2 hours and requires basic tools. YouTube has model-specific tutorials for virtually every opener. A professional charges $100 to $200 for the repair. If the opener is more than 15 years old and the gear has stripped, consider replacing the entire opener. See our [best garage door openers guide](/reviews/best-garage-door-openers) for recommendations.

### Cause 8: Roller, Hinge, or Hardware Failure

Fix: $10 — $200

Rollers, hinges, and brackets can wear out, seize, or break. A seized roller creates a binding point that the opener cannot push through. A broken hinge allows a panel to shift out of alignment. Both can prevent the door from closing.

Symptoms:

  * Door binds or sticks at a specific point
  * Visible broken roller (cracked wheel, bent stem)
  * Squealing, grinding, or popping sounds during operation
  * A hinge is visibly broken or a panel is sagging

How to fix it:

Nylon or steel rollers are inexpensive ($5 to $10 each) and can be replaced by removing the hinge bracket, sliding out the old roller, and inserting a new one. **Do NOT remove the bottom bracket on either side of the door** as it is connected to the cable under spring tension. Hinges are similarly replaceable. If multiple rollers are worn, replace them all at once. A full set of 10 to 12 rollers costs $30 to $60 for nylon or $50 to $100 for sealed-bearing steel.

Professional roller replacement (full set): $150 to $200.

### Cause 9: Lock Mode Engaged

Fix: $0 • Time: 10 seconds

Some openers have a lock or vacation mode that disables the remote control. When engaged, pressing the remote does nothing but the wall button may still work (or neither may work, depending on the model).

Symptoms:

  * Remote does not work
  * A lock icon is visible on the wall control panel
  * The opener's light may flash in a specific pattern indicating lock mode

How to fix it:

Press and hold the lock button on the wall control for 2 to 3 seconds until the lock icon disappears. The remote should work again immediately. Check your opener's manual if you cannot locate the lock button.

### Cause 10: Power or Wiring Issue

Fix: $0 — $300

If the opener has no power, nothing works. But partial power issues — corroded connections, a tripped GFCI outlet, or damaged low-voltage wiring — can cause intermittent or unpredictable behavior.

Symptoms:

  * Opener does not respond to any input (remote, wall button, or app)
  * Opener lights are off
  * Opener works sometimes but not others
  * GFCI outlet has tripped (test/reset buttons on the outlet)

How to fix it:

  1. **Check the GFCI outlet.** Many garages have GFCI-protected outlets. Press the reset button. If it trips again immediately, you have an electrical issue that needs an electrician.
  2. **Check the breaker.** Verify the garage circuit breaker has not tripped.
  3. **Check the outlet.** Plug a lamp or phone charger into the same outlet to verify it has power.
  4. **Check wall button wiring.** The low-voltage wires connecting the wall button to the opener can come loose. Verify both wires are securely attached at both ends.

Cost: $0 for breaker or GFCI reset. $100 to $300 for electrician if wiring repair is needed.

## DIY vs. Professional: When to Call a Pro

Fix| DIY?| Why
---|---|---
Clean or realign sensors| Yes| No tools needed, 5 minutes
Replace remote battery| Yes| 2 minutes
Clear track obstruction| Yes| Visual check and cleanup
Adjust limit or force settings| Yes| Screwdriver, follow manual
Disengage lock mode| Yes| Press a button
Reset GFCI or breaker| Yes| Press a button
Replace sensors| Yes| Two screws and two wires per sensor
Replace rollers (except bottom brackets)| Yes (careful)| Basic tools, 30 min per roller
Replace drive gear| Maybe| Moderate DIY, 1 to 2 hours
Minor track straightening| Maybe| Rubber mallet, go gently
Spring or cable replacement| Never| Extreme tension, serious injury risk
Major track repair or replacement| No| Requires specialized tools and alignment
Electrical wiring repair| No| Licensed electrician required

For doors with multiple recurring issues that suggest end-of-life, use our [garage door replacement cost calculator](/cost-guides/garage-door-replacement-cost-calculator) to estimate the cost of replacing the full door system.

## How to Close Your Garage Door in an Emergency

If your door is stuck open and you need to secure it right now:

  1. **Pull the emergency release cord** — the red handle hanging from the trolley on the rail. This disconnects the door from the opener.
  2. **Manually lower the door by hand.** If the springs are intact, the door should feel manageable (30 to 50 pounds of effort). If a spring is broken, the door will be very heavy (100 to 400 pounds). Get help and lower it carefully.
  3. **Lock the door from inside** using the manual slide lock on the inside of the door if equipped, or place a C-clamp or locking pliers on the track just above one of the rollers to prevent the door from being opened from outside.
  4. **Call for repair.** Do not attempt to re-engage the opener until the underlying problem is fixed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my garage door start to close then immediately reverse?+

This is almost always a safety sensor problem — the #1 cause 80% of the time. The two photo-eye sensors near the floor are blocked, dirty, or misaligned. Check that both sensor indicator lights are steady (amber on the sender, green on the receiver). Clean the lenses, remove any obstructions, and adjust alignment until both lights are solid.

My garage door won't close with the remote but closes if I hold the wall button. What's wrong?+

This is a classic safety sensor failure. Holding the wall button manually overrides the sensors on most openers. The sensors themselves are failing, dirty, or misaligned. Clean and realign them first. If the indicator lights are both steady but the problem persists, replace the sensors ($15 to $50).

How do I close my garage door when the opener is broken?+

Pull the red emergency release cord hanging from the trolley on the rail. This disconnects the door from the opener. Manually lower the door — if the springs are intact it should feel manageable (30 to 50 lbs). If springs are broken, the door will be very heavy (100 to 400 lbs); get help. Once closed, lock it with the manual slide lock or a C-clamp on the track above a roller.

Why does my garage door reverse right before it hits the floor?+

The close-limit setting is telling the opener the door has already reached the ground before it actually has, so it reverses to avoid crushing something. Adjust the close-limit screw (labeled “down” or “close” on the opener unit) in small quarter-turn increments. Test after each adjustment. On smart openers the limit may be set in the app.

How much does it cost to fix a garage door that won't close?+

Most causes cost $0 to $50 to fix: sensor cleaning and alignment ($0), remote battery ($3 to $5), limit or force adjustment ($0), clearing track obstructions ($0), replacing sensors ($15 to $50). Spring replacement costs $150 to $350 professionally. A new opener costs $200 to $400 installed. The average service call is $75 to $150 plus parts. See our [garage door replacement cost guide](/cost-guides/garage-door-replacement-cost) if the door itself needs replacing.

Can I bypass the safety sensors permanently?+

Technically yes, but you should never do this. Safety sensors (photo eyes) are a federal requirement under [UL 325](https://www.ul.com/news/ul-325-50th-anniversary-key-safety-issues) that prevent the door from closing on people, pets, and objects. Bypassing them creates a serious injury risk and may void your homeowner's insurance. Fix or replace the sensors instead.

Why won't my garage door close in cold weather?+

Cold causes metal tracks to contract slightly, lubricant to thicken, and weatherstripping to stiffen — all increasing resistance. Try increasing the force setting slightly and apply a silicone-based lubricant (not WD-40) to tracks, rollers, and hinges. If the problem only happens in extreme cold, the springs may be weakening near end of life.

Should I replace my garage door opener or just repair it?+

If the opener is under 10 years old, repair is usually worthwhile. If it is over 15 years old and has a stripped gear, failing logic board, or no safety features (no battery backup, no smartphone connectivity), replacement is the better investment. Modern openers are significantly quieter, more secure, and more reliable. See our [best garage door openers guide](/reviews/best-garage-door-openers).

## Glossary

Safety sensors (photo-eyes)

Infrared sensors mounted near the floor on each side of the garage door opening. Required on all automatic openers since 1993. They detect obstructions and prevent the door from closing on objects, people, or pets.

Close-limit setting

A control on the opener that defines how far the door travels downward before the motor stops. If set incorrectly, the door may reverse before reaching the floor or push too hard against it.

Force setting

A control on the opener that defines how much resistance the motor will push through before reversing. Prevents the door from crushing objects but must be set high enough to overcome normal friction.

Torsion spring

A tightly wound spring mounted on a shaft above the garage door opening. Stores energy when the door closes and releases it to assist opening. Under extreme tension. Professional replacement only.

Extension spring

A spring mounted along the horizontal track on each side of the door. Stretches when the door closes and contracts to assist opening. Less dangerous than torsion springs but still carries significant force.

Trolley

The carriage that connects the garage door arm to the chain, belt, or screw drive on the opener rail. The emergency release cord disconnects the trolley, allowing manual door operation.

Drive gear

A nylon or plastic gear inside the opener that transfers motor rotation to the drive mechanism. Wears over time and eventually strips, causing the motor to run without moving the door.

GFCI (Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter)

A type of electrical outlet with built-in protection that trips when it detects a ground fault. Common in garages. A tripped GFCI cuts power to the opener. Reset by pressing the reset button on the outlet.
